why_use_this: This is the general-purpose numerical-methods toolbox most other packages in the vani-* math ecosystem either depend on or duplicate a piece of ([vani-algebra](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-algebra), [vani-interval](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-interval), [vani-vectorcalc](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-vectorcalc) all reuse or mirror functions from here). Reach for it whenever you need to integrate, differentiate, find a root, minimize a 1D function, solve an ODE, work with polynomials, or interpolate between sample points, and a compiler builtin (`sin`, `exp`, `f64_erf`, ...) doesn't already cover it directly. For ODEs specifically: use the explicit solvers (`euler_solve`, `rk4_solve`, `rk45_step`) for well-behaved ("non-stiff") systems, but switch to the implicit solvers (`backward_euler_solve`, `crank_nicolson_solve`, `bdf2_solve`) for STIFF systems -- ones where the explicit solvers diverge or need an impractically tiny step size to stay stable, since the implicit methods are unconditionally stable (A-stable) at the cost of solving a small nonlinear equation via Newton's method at every step.

math_notes.integrate_trapz: The trapezoidal rule: \( \displaystyle\int_a^b f\,dx \approx \dfrac{h}{2}\left(y_0 + 2y_1 + \cdots + 2y_{n-1} + y_n\right) \) for \( n \) equal subintervals of width \( h=(b-a)/n \) -- approximates the area under each subinterval as a trapezoid.
math_notes.integrate_simpson: Composite Simpson's rule: \( \displaystyle\int_a^b f\,dx \approx \dfrac{h}{3}\left(y_0 + 4y_1 + 2y_2 + 4y_3 + \cdots + 4y_{n-1} + y_n\right) \) for an EVEN number of subintervals -- fits a parabola through each consecutive triple of points instead of a straight line, exact for any cubic or lower-degree polynomial.
math_notes.integrate_romberg: Romberg integration: builds a triangular table of trapezoidal-rule estimates at successively halved step sizes, then applies Richardson extrapolation across the table (each column cancels one more order of the error term) to reach much higher accuracy than any single trapezoidal estimate -- the same idea that makes `bdf2_step` second-order from two first-order-ish pieces, applied to integration instead of ODEs.
math_notes.integrate_gauss_legendre_5: 5-point Gauss-Legendre quadrature: \( \displaystyle\int_a^b f\,dx \approx \dfrac{b-a}{2}\sum_{i=1}^5 w_i f(x_i) \) using the 5 fixed Gauss-Legendre nodes/weights on \( [-1,1] \) mapped onto \( [a,b] \) -- exact for polynomials up to degree 9, far higher accuracy per function evaluation than Simpson's rule for smooth functions.
math_notes.integrate_adaptive_trapz: Recursively bisects \( [a,b] \), comparing the trapezoidal estimate over the whole interval against the sum of the two half-interval estimates -- when they agree within `tol`, accepts the finer estimate; when they don't, recurses into both halves -- concentrates evaluation effort where \( f \) is changing fastest instead of using a uniform grid.
math_notes.diff_central: \( f'(x) \approx \dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x-h)}{2h} \) -- the central-difference derivative estimate, \( O(h^2) \) accurate (error shrinks quadratically as \( h\to 0 \)), more accurate than the one-sided `diff_forward` for the same \( h \).
math_notes.diff_forward: \( f'(x) \approx \dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} \) -- the one-sided forward-difference estimate, only \( O(h) \) accurate (error shrinks linearly), needed when you can't evaluate \( f \) below \( x \) (e.g. at a domain boundary).
math_notes.diff_second: \( f''(x) \approx \dfrac{f(x-h) - 2f(x) + f(x+h)}{h^2} \) -- the standard 3-point central second-derivative stencil, the same one [vani-vectorcalc](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-vectorcalc)'s `vc_laplacian_2d` and [vani-pde](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-pde)'s heat/Laplace solvers build on.
math_notes.bisect: The bisection root-finding method: given \( f(a) \) and \( f(b) \) with opposite signs (guaranteeing a root lies between them by the intermediate value theorem), repeatedly evaluate the midpoint and keep whichever half still brackets a sign change -- guaranteed to converge, halving the bracket width every iteration, but only linearly (the slowest of this package's root-finders).
math_notes.secant: The secant method: \( x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)\dfrac{x_n - x_{n-1}}{f(x_n)-f(x_{n-1})} \) -- approximates Newton's method's derivative with a finite difference between the two most recent points instead of requiring an analytic derivative; superlinear convergence (order \( \approx 1.618 \), the golden ratio) but not guaranteed to converge the way bisection is.
math_notes.newton: Newton's method for root-finding: \( x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n) \) -- quadratic convergence near a simple root (error roughly squares each step) when it converges, but can diverge or cycle from a bad starting point, unlike bisection's guaranteed-but-slow convergence.
math_notes.brent: Brent's method: combines bisection's guaranteed convergence with the speed of secant/inverse-quadratic interpolation, falling back to a bisection step whenever the faster method's step would leave the current bracket or converge too slowly -- the practical "best of both worlds" root-finder, and the only one of this package's root-finders with that guarantee.
math_notes.golden_section: Golden-section search for 1D minimization: narrows a bracket \( [a,b] \) known to contain a minimum by evaluating \( f \) at two interior points placed at the golden ratio \( \varphi = (\sqrt5-1)/2 \approx 0.618 \) fraction of the interval -- this specific ratio means one of the two evaluated points can always be reused in the next iteration, so each iteration costs only one new function evaluation.
math_notes.brent_min: Brent's method for 1D minimization: combines golden-section search's guaranteed bracket-narrowing with parabolic interpolation's faster convergence when the function looks locally quadratic, falling back to golden section whenever the parabolic step isn't trustworthy -- the minimization analog of `brent`'s root-finding combination.
math_notes.newton_min: Newton's method applied to minimization: \( x_{n+1} = x_n - f'(x_n)/f''(x_n) \), i.e. Newton's root-finding method applied to \( f' \) instead of \( f \) (a minimum is where the derivative is zero) -- quadratic convergence near a minimum where \( f'' > 0 \), but like root-finding Newton, not guaranteed to converge from an arbitrary start.
math_notes.euler_solve: Forward (explicit) Euler: \( y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(t_n, y_n) \) -- the simplest possible ODE step, only first-order accurate and only CONDITIONALLY stable (can blow up on stiff problems even with a seemingly reasonable step size).
math_notes.rk4_solve: Classical 4th-order Runge-Kutta: \( y_{n+1} = y_n + \tfrac{h}{6}(k_1+2k_2+2k_3+k_4) \), where \( k_1,\ldots,k_4 \) are four function evaluations at cleverly chosen intermediate points across the step -- fourth-order accurate (error shrinks as \( h^4 \)) for a cost of 4 evaluations per step, the standard general-purpose explicit ODE solver.
math_notes.rk45_step: Runge-Kutta-Fehlberg (RK45): computes both a 4th-order and a 5th-order estimate from the same set of function evaluations, so their DIFFERENCE gives a built-in local error estimate a caller could use for adaptive step-size control -- a more sophisticated single step than plain RK4, though this function returns just the step's value.
math_notes.adams_bashforth_2: The 2-step Adams-Bashforth multistep method: \( y_{n+1} = y_n + \tfrac{h}{2}\big(3f(t_n,y_n) - f(t_{n-1},y_{n-1})\big) \) -- reuses the PREVIOUS step's already-computed \( f \) value instead of evaluating \( f \) fresh multiple times per step the way RK4 does, cheaper per step but needs a separate method (like Euler) to bootstrap its first point.
math_notes.backward_euler_step: Backward (implicit) Euler: \( y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(t_{n+1}, y_{n+1}) \) -- note \( y_{n+1} \) appears on BOTH sides, so this is a nonlinear equation solved via Newton's method (with a central-difference derivative) rather than evaluated directly. Unconditionally stable (A-stable): stays bounded for a stiff system regardless of step size, unlike forward Euler, at the cost of an implicit solve every step.
math_notes.crank_nicolson_step: The Crank-Nicolson (trapezoidal) implicit method: \( y_{n+1} = y_n + \tfrac{h}{2}\big(f(t_n,y_n) + f(t_{n+1},y_{n+1})\big) \) -- averages the derivative at both endpoints of the step (also solved via Newton's method, since \( y_{n+1} \) appears on both sides), second-order accurate unlike backward Euler's first order, while keeping the same unconditional A-stability.
math_notes.bdf2_step: The 2-step Backward Differentiation Formula: \( y_{n+1} = \tfrac{4}{3}y_n - \tfrac{1}{3}y_{n-1} + \tfrac{2h}{3}f(t_{n+1}, y_{n+1}) \) -- another implicit, A-stable, second-order-accurate method like Crank-Nicolson, but derived from fitting a backward-difference polynomial through 3 points instead of trapezoidal averaging; needs the two PRIOR points, so `bdf2_solve` bootstraps its first step via `backward_euler_step`.
math_notes.poly_eval: \( p(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{n} c_i x^i \), evaluated via Horner's method (\( ((c_n x + c_{n-1})x + c_{n-2})x + \cdots \)) rather than computing each power \( x^i \) separately -- \( n \) multiply-adds instead of \( O(n^2) \) naive power computation.
math_notes.poly_deriv_coeffs: \( p'(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} i\,c_i x^{i-1} \) -- the coefficient-by-coefficient power rule, returning the derivative polynomial's coefficients directly (one degree lower) rather than a numeric value at a point.
math_notes.poly_mul: Polynomial multiplication via convolution of coefficient arrays: \( (p \cdot q)_k = \sum_{i+j=k} p_i q_j \) -- the coefficient of \( x^k \) in the product is the sum of every pair of input coefficients whose exponents add to \( k \), the standard \( O(n^2) \) schoolbook polynomial multiply (same asymptotic shape as `bn_mul` in [vani-bignum](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-bignum), just over `f64` coefficients instead of base-\(10^9\) digit limbs).
math_notes.lagrange_interp: The Lagrange interpolation formula: \( p(x) = \sum_{i} y_i \prod_{j \ne i} \dfrac{x - x_j}{x_i - x_j} \) -- the unique degree-\((n-1)\) polynomial passing through all \( n \) given points, evaluated directly at a single query point \( x \) without ever forming the polynomial's coefficients explicitly.
math_notes.cubic_spline_natural: Builds a natural cubic spline through the given points: a piecewise-cubic curve that's continuous in value, first derivative, AND second derivative across every knot (unlike Lagrange interpolation, which can oscillate wildly for many points), with the "natural" boundary condition that the second derivative is zero at both endpoints -- solves a tridiagonal linear system for the second-derivative values \( M_i \) at each knot, which `cubic_spline_eval` then uses.
math_notes.cubic_spline_eval: Evaluates the natural cubic spline `cubic_spline_natural` built, at a query point \( x \): finds which interval \( [x_i, x_{i+1}] \) contains \( x \) (via binary search, hence the \( \log_2 n \) cost) and evaluates that interval's cubic piece using its endpoint values and the precomputed second-derivatives \( M_i, M_{i+1} \).
math_notes.kahan_sum: Kahan summation: accumulates a running sum while separately tracking and correcting for the floating-point rounding error lost at each addition, giving a far more accurate total than naively summing left-to-right when adding many `f64` values -- particularly when the values being summed have very different magnitudes.
math_notes.running_mean_update: \( \bar{x}_n = \bar{x}_{n-1} + \dfrac{x - \bar{x}_{n-1}}{n} \) -- updates a running mean by one new sample without needing to re-sum every prior value, mathematically equivalent to the plain average but computed incrementally.
